title: Predicates, nulls and types
subtitle: Specify the exact rows first: three-valued logic, precise boundaries and typed comparisons.
objectives: Predict true, false and unknown in WHERE
Keep null handling explicit rather than replacing missing data
Use exact numeric and half-open timestamp comparisons
Separate expression semantics from the planner's evaluation choices

exercises.title: Choose an exact amount interval
exercises.prompt: Return id and total for paid orders with a known total at least 100 and strictly below 240. Order by id. Do not include either unknown totals or the upper boundary.
exercises.solution_sql: SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND total >= 100 AND total < 240 ORDER BY id
exercises.explanation: The lower bound is inclusive and the upper bound exclusive. BETWEEN would include 240. Comparisons with an unknown total yield unknown and WHERE keeps only true.

exercises.title: Preserve the missing amount deliberately
exercises.prompt: Return id and total for paid orders whose total is at least 100 or is unknown. Exclude all other statuses, including unknown totals belonging to pending orders. Order by id.
exercises.solution_sql: SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND (total >= 100 OR total IS NULL) ORDER BY id
exercises.explanation: Parentheses make the intended grouping explicit. Without them, AND binds more tightly than OR and an unknown total from a different status can enter the result. Treating an unknown amount as zero would discard required rows.

exercises.title: Expose the third truth value
exercises.prompt: For every order return id, above_100 equal to the expression total > 100, and amount_missing equal to total IS NULL. Preserve unknown as SQL null in above_100. Order by id.
exercises.solution_sql: SELECT id, total > 100 AS above_100, total IS NULL AS amount_missing FROM orders ORDER BY id
exercises.explanation: Projection makes all three truth values visible. IS NULL always produces true or false; an ordinary comparison with null produces unknown. COALESCE(total > 100, false) changes the requested result.

exercises.title: Compare without losing nulls
exercises.prompt: Return id and total for all orders whose total is distinct from 100. This must include orders with an unknown total, and exclude orders with total exactly 100. Order by id.
exercises.solution_sql: SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE total IS DISTINCT FROM 100 ORDER BY id
exercises.explanation: IS DISTINCT FROM treats null as a comparable missing value for this operation. Ordinary <> returns unknown for a null input and WHERE would omit it. The equivalent explicit disjunction total <> 100 OR total IS NULL is also valid here.

exercises.title: Use a half-open time window
exercises.prompt: Return id and ordered_at for orders placed from 2026-01-01 00:00:00 UTC inclusive to 2026-01-08 00:00:00 UTC exclusive. Include every status and order by ordered_at, then id. Compare timestamps rather than formatted strings.
exercises.solution_sql: SELECT id, ordered_at FROM orders WHERE ordered_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00' AND ordered_at < TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-08 00:00:00+00' ORDER BY ordered_at, id
exercises.explanation: Adjacent half-open windows neither overlap nor leave gaps. An explicit UTC offset fixes the intended instants. A last-millisecond upper bound depends on precision and is unnecessary.

exercises.title: Keep the comparison numeric
exercises.prompt: Return id and total for every order with a known total strictly greater than 100, regardless of status. Keep total numeric in the result and order by total ascending, then id. Do not compare the textual rendering of total.
exercises.solution_sql: SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE total > NUMERIC '100' ORDER BY total, id
exercises.explanation: Numeric order differs from lexicographic order: the text '80' sorts after '100' while the number 80 is smaller. Keeping the column numeric also leaves a matching numeric index usable when the planner judges it worthwhile.

transcript: A query can be fast, syntactically valid, and wrong. This chapter concentrates on the contract that every later optimization must preserve. We will use the same orders table, but add exact boundaries, missing amounts, and a time window. Before opening a plan, write down which rows belong in the answer. Include a row exactly on each boundary, a row just outside, a missing value, and a tie. These are small examples with large consequences. When an optimizer changes a predicate or an application rewrites a query, these cases tell us whether the meaning survived. A favorable timing number cannot rescue a different answer.

Start with total greater than one hundred. For a total of one hundred and twenty-five, the comparison is true. For eighty, it is false. For a missing amount, PostgreSQL does not invent a number; the result is unknown, represented by SQL null. WHERE retains rows whose predicate is true. Both false and unknown are excluded. Run a projection of the comparison itself, alongside total IS NULL. This exposes the distinction that a WHERE clause hides. The comparison can contain null, while the missing-value predicate returns a definite Boolean. Understanding that difference is more useful than memorizing a special spelling for null.

Equality with null is not a missing-value test. Neither total equals null nor total differs from null identifies the rows you intend. Their result is unknown. Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to test whether the value is missing. Do not replace unknown amounts with zero simply to make a predicate easier. Missing and zero can mean different things in the application. A sum normally skips null inputs, while COUNT of a column skips those inputs and COUNT star counts rows. The choice must come from the result contract. It cannot come from whichever expression happens to produce a convenient sample answer.

Boolean combinations also have a third value. True AND unknown is unknown. False AND unknown is false. True OR unknown is true. False OR unknown is unknown. NOT unknown remains unknown. You can inspect these cases using a VALUES relation containing true, false and a Boolean null, then project the combinations. The important consequence is that a predicate can be neither true nor false without being an execution error. This becomes especially important when we later study anti joins, nullable foreign keys, and NOT IN. For now, keep the third value visible in your reasoning rather than mentally treating it as false everywhere.

Suppose the business rule is paid orders whose amount is at least one hundred, including paid orders with an unknown amount so that someone can investigate them. The expression is status equals paid AND, in parentheses, amount at least one hundred OR amount IS NULL. The parentheses communicate the contract. Without them, AND binds more tightly than OR, so an unknown amount from a pending order can leak into the result. The incorrect query may look right when the visible fixture has no such pending row. This is why the assessment changes the data. We need evidence that the query represents the rule, not evidence that it happens to match one convenient sample.

Sometimes the rule really does ask whether two values differ, including missing values. IS DISTINCT FROM provides that comparison. For total compared with one hundred, an unknown total is distinct from the known number. One hundred is not distinct from itself. IS NOT DISTINCT FROM gives the complementary comparison and considers two nulls alike for this purpose. Ordinary equals and not-equals retain their three-valued behavior. Choose the operation that matches the rule. These operators become useful in synchronization, change detection, and joins over nullable keys. They are not a universal replacement for equality, and a later index investigation must inspect the actual supported operator and chosen access path.

Next make an amount interval exact. At least one hundred and strictly below two hundred and forty is a lower-inclusive, upper-exclusive interval. BETWEEN includes both endpoints, so it expresses a different rule. A strict comparison and an inclusive comparison are not interchangeable merely because the current fixture lacks the boundary value. Write down the two inequalities separately. Then check one hundred, two hundred and forty, a value below one hundred, and a missing amount. Decimal numeric values preserve this contract without a binary floating-point approximation. The type of the stored column and the type selected for the comparison both matter.

A value's printed form is not its comparison semantics. Numeric eighty is below one hundred. The text eighty, beginning with the character eight, can sort after text beginning with one. Casting total to text before comparing it changes the operation. A literal initially written in quotes can be resolved to a type by context; that is different from explicitly forcing the column into a textual representation. Inspect pg_typeof in a scratch query when the type is unclear. In the exercise, keep total numeric in the result as well. A grader that compared only printed strings could miss a type error, so our result checks retain type information and normalize equivalent numeric scales.

Time windows need the same boundary discipline. Use the beginning instant inclusive and the next beginning instant exclusive. A week starting at midnight January first UTC ends before midnight January eighth UTC. Adjacent windows then fit together without double-counting their boundary. Do not guess a final millisecond or append a series of nines. PostgreSQL can store timestamps with finer precision than that assumption, and applications can change precision. A half-open interval states the actual rule directly. Test a row at the lower boundary, at the upper boundary, just before each, and with a different display time zone.

The orders column is timestamp with time zone, which PostgreSQL uses to represent an instant. Its textual display depends on the session time zone. Our lab fixes the session to UTC and our constants contain an explicit UTC offset. That keeps the lesson reproducible. Timestamp without time zone has different semantics: it describes a date and clock time without automatically identifying an instant. Do not mix these casually and then treat a display difference as a storage change. When a report asks for a business-local day, compute the corresponding instant boundaries deliberately. Daylight-saving transitions are a reason to define the business rule carefully, not a reason to compare formatted date strings.

The order in which you write Boolean terms is not a promise about their evaluation order. PostgreSQL can reorganize expressions during planning and execution. Do not use an earlier term as a general-purpose guard against a later division by zero or failing cast. Where conditional evaluation is needed, use an appropriate conditional expression and understand its limits, including expressions that can be folded at planning time. We will investigate expression execution much later in the course. The practical habit now is simpler: write predicates for their meaning, and use plan evidence for the implementation. SQL clause order is not a line-by-line imperative program.

Once the answer is precise, inspect the predicate's physical consequences. The filter selectivity affects how many rows a scan is expected to emit. A comparison directly on a numeric column can support a matching numeric index. Applying a transformation to the column can require a matching expression index or a different rewrite. Neither observation guarantees that an index is chosen. On our tiny fixture, reading the whole table can be cheaper than following an index. Explain shows the chosen estimate; Analyze runs the query and shows actual rows. The absence of an index scan is not evidence that your predicate is wrong or that PostgreSQL ignored the index.

Use a controlled comparison rather than changing several things at once. Run the numeric predicate and its textual counterpart, inspect their results, and then inspect their plans. If the results differ, stop: this is not a valid optimization experiment. If two forms preserve the required result, compare their estimates and measured work on the same fixture. Later we will add larger and skewed distributions, which can change the chosen plan without changing the meaning. The unit of correctness is the required result, including duplicates, nulls and requested order. The unit of performance evidence is work measured under stated conditions.

The six exercises make these contracts concrete. Specify an exact amount interval. Parenthesize a business rule that deliberately preserves missing paid amounts. Project true, false and unknown rather than hiding them in WHERE. Compare values with IS DISTINCT FROM. Define a UTC window using half-open bounds. Finally keep a numeric comparison numeric. Run your own diagnostic queries as often as needed, but submit the requested result shape for checking. The reference answer stays collapsed until you try. It explains why the result is correct; it is not the only accepted SQL spelling. Keep the boundary cases in mind as we move into joins, where one small semantic mistake can multiply across thousands of rows.
